plot_extraction.response_text:
A stubborn little girl named Kitty receives new shoes that become magical on midsummer day. Whenever she refuses an errand, disobeys, or acts unkindly, the shoes force her to do what is right, whisking her to the kitchen, post office, school, garden, and other destinations. They also prevent her from stealing cake, dawdling, and kicking down another child’s toy. When Kitty willingly helps others, however, the shoes reward her with extraordinary leaps and graceful dancing.

Kitty eventually chooses to run charitable errands pleasantly, delivering clothes, books, food, and money to families in need. Afterward, she visits a grove called Fairyland, where the shoes allow her to understand the speech of animals and insects. At sunset their magic ends, but Kitty remembers their lessons. She becomes more obedient and helpful, learns to dance beautifully, and develops a lasting affection for the creatures of the woods and fields.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the style of a nineteenth-century didactic fairy tale for children, combining domestic realism with light fantasy and an explicit moral purpose. Its world is familiar and orderly—home, school, errands, meals, charitable visits—but a single magical device, the enchanted “skipping shoes,” transforms ordinary duties into comic adventures. The fantasy is playful rather than threatening: the shoes discipline Kitty by physically compelling her to obey, while also rewarding kindness and willing cooperation with graceful dancing, extraordinary leaps, and access to the voices of woodland creatures. This gives the narrative the character of a moral lesson disguised as an entertaining day-long escapade.

The narrator is third-person omniscient and strongly authoritative, speaking with the confidence of an adult storyteller addressing young readers. Kitty’s actions and thoughts are freely reported, while the narrator occasionally offers general moral commentary, as in the observation that people feel happy after doing kind things. The opening immediately defines Kitty by her fault—she habitually says “I won’t” and “I can’t”—and contrasts her with “obliging children,” establishing the behavioral standard against which she will be judged. The tone remains affectionate rather than severe. Kitty is called naughty, cross, and disobedient, but her flaws are treated as correctable childish habits, and her punishment is humorous, proportionate, and ultimately beneficial.

The prose is clear, linear, and accessible, with moderately long sentences linked by semicolons, conjunctions, and sequential clauses. The diction is simple but distinctly period-flavored, using terms such as “mamma,” “Nursey,” “victuals,” “piazza,” “cosey,” and “oblige.” Repeated temporal and causal formulas—“One day,” “The words were hardly out of her mouth,” “The minute she gave up,” and “When all the errands were done”—create the smooth forward motion of oral storytelling. Repetition is central to the comic pattern: Kitty begins a refusal, the shoes instantly act, and she is carried to the place where duty requires her to go. Variations on “I won’t,” “I can’t,” “away went the shoes,” and “at one jump” give the story a refrain-like quality and reinforce its lesson without complicated explanation.

Dialogue is frequent, brief, and vividly characterizing. Kitty’s complaints, unfinished protests, sighs, and private remarks convey impulsiveness and self-dramatization, while her mother speaks calmly and persuasively. The adults generally guide rather than threaten her, and the mother’s decision to let Kitty “choose” whether to perform the charitable errands marks the decisive stage in her reform. Much of the humor comes from the discrepancy between Kitty’s words and her body: she declares that she cannot or will not move, while the shoes leap, trot, dance, or drag her onward. Exclamation marks, abrupt interruptions, and broken-off phrases such as “I’m too ti—” heighten the speed and physical comedy.

The plot has an episodic, cumulative structure. Each episode tests a related failing: reluctance to help, temptation to steal cake, distraction, lateness, anger, selfishness, or resistance to duty. At first the shoes operate as an external corrective, preventing forbidden actions and forcing obedience. Kitty then discovers their positive power when she offers to help another child and is rewarded with a marvelous leap. The emotional turning point comes when she voluntarily agrees to carry supplies to poor families. From then on, movement becomes easy and harmonious, indicating that her will has aligned with the lesson represented by the shoes. The day closes when the magic expires at sunset, restoring ordinary reality while preserving the habits and sympathies Kitty has acquired.

Imagery is concrete, bright, and animated. The shoes wink with button-like eyes, tap tunes with their heels, and seem to possess a mischievous personality. Movement verbs—“skipped,” “trotted,” “whisked,” “dragged,” “pranced,” and “waltzing”—sustain a buoyant kinetic energy. The Fairyland passage shifts into more lyrical nature writing, with fern arches, moss, wood flowers, squirrels, butterflies, frogs, and birds forming a miniature enchanted society. Similes are child-friendly and visual: Kitty moves like a grasshopper or an india-rubber ball; hungry children gather like young birds; the setting sun resembles the wink of a sleepy eye. Nature is both magical and educational, encouraging sympathy for “innocent and interesting little creatures.”

The governing themes are willing obedience, self-control, usefulness, kindness, and the transformation of duty into pleasure. The story distinguishes coerced goodness from chosen goodness: Kitty initially behaves properly only because the shoes compel her, but gradually learns that cheerful service brings freedom, delight, and social approval. Its moral is overt yet softened by comedy, sensory charm, and wish-fulfillment. Overall, the style is warm, brisk, whimsical, and gently corrective, with a strong domestic ethic and a child-centered fantasy mechanism that makes moral education visible through physical action.

## Kitty’s Skipping Shoes

Kitty was a dear little girl in many respects; she had bright eyes, rosy cheeks, and a laugh that made the house seem merry. But she possessed one very disagreeable habit. Whenever she was asked to do anything, she nearly always answered, “I can’t,” or, “I won’t.”

If mamma said, “Kitty, please carry this spool of cotton to Nursey,” Kitty would reply, “I can’t; I am busy.”

If papa said, “Run and bring me my spectacles, dear,” she would pout and say, “I won’t; they are too far away.”

The spectacles might be only across the room, and her important business might be dressing a paper doll; but Kitty thought her own wishes should always come first. This is a great mistake, as all obliging children know.

One summer morning, a little parcel came home from the shoemaker’s. In it was a pair of red shoes, with shining black buttons and small heels that made the pleasantest tap upon the floor.

Kitty clapped her hands.

“Oh, mamma, are they mine?”

“Yes,” said mamma. “They are for midsummer day. Try them on.”

Kitty thrust in one foot and then the other. The shoes fitted exactly. Indeed, they seemed to hug her toes in a friendly manner; and when Nursey fastened the last button, Kitty thought she saw both shoes give a sly little wink.

“What funny shoes!” she cried.

“They are very pretty,” said mamma. “Now take this basket to Cook, if you please.”

“I won’t go down to the kit—”

The words were hardly out of her mouth before the red shoes gave one jump, whisked Kitty through the nursery door, skipped down the passage, and carried her over the stairs so rapidly that she had no time to count them. At the kitchen threshold they stopped with a firm little stamp.

Cook looked up from her pastry.

“Well, miss, you have come quickly.”

“I didn’t come,” said Kitty indignantly. “The shoes brought me.”

Cook laughed, supposing this to be one of Kitty’s fancies, and took the basket.

“Since you are here, carry this bunch of parsley to your mamma.”

“I can’t. I am too ti—”

Away went the shoes! They sprang upstairs, trotted along the passage, and landed Kitty beside mamma’s chair, with the parsley held straight before her like a green bouquet.

“Thank you, dear,” said mamma.

Kitty stared at her feet. The black buttons certainly winked again.

“I don’t like you,” she whispered.

Tap, tap, answered the heels, as if they did not care in the least.

After breakfast mamma gave Kitty a letter.

“Please post this on your way to school.”

“I shall forget it,” said Kitty.

“Put it safely in your pocket.”

Kitty did so, but when she reached the garden gate she saw a yellow butterfly and ran after it. The butterfly fluttered over the lavender, rested upon a rose, and sailed across the lawn. Kitty followed until she was far from the road.

“I knew I should forget that tiresome letter,” she said.

Instantly the shoes turned about. They rushed through the gate, pattered down the lane, and carried Kitty straight to the post office. She tried to catch at a hedge; but the twigs only scratched her fingers, while the shoes trotted faster than ever.

“I won’t post it!” she cried, pressing both hands over her pocket.

The right shoe began to climb the post-office step; the left gave a determined skip; and Kitty’s hand, in trying to keep her balance, flew from her pocket. Out came the letter. Before she knew what had happened, it was through the opening.

“There!” said Kitty. “You are the most meddlesome shoes in the world.”

The heels tapped a merry tune.

They then hurried her toward school, for it was nearly nine o’clock. Kitty wished to stop at the brook and sail a leaf under the bridge.

“There is plenty of time,” she said, though she knew there was not.

The shoes refused to turn aside. They flew along the road, skipped over a muddy place at one jump, and deposited her at the schoolroom door just as the bell rang.

During the morning Kitty behaved tolerably well, chiefly because she feared what the shoes might do. Once she whispered to Lucy Gray when she should have been attending to her sums; but the shoes rapped sharply beneath the desk, and the teacher looked in that direction. Kitty immediately bent over her slate.

At noon, on her way home, she met a small boy named Robin building a house of sticks beside the road. He had made four neat walls, a gateway, and a little garden marked out with pebbles.

Kitty was cross because she had missed two sums.

“What a stupid house!” she said.

“It is not finished,” answered Robin. “The roof is to be made of moss.”

“I can kick it down with one foot.”

She lifted her right shoe; but instead of striking the house, it leaped completely over Robin, while the left followed so briskly that Kitty turned a somersault upon the grass.

Robin laughed, though he politely tried to hide it.

Kitty rose, red and angry.

“I will do it this time!”

Again she raised her foot, and again the shoe sprang over the little house. This leap was higher than the first, and Kitty landed in a patch of soft clover six yards away.

The shoes would not permit mischief, however much their owner desired it.

Presently a gust of wind scattered Robin’s pile of moss.

“Oh!” he cried. “Now I must fetch it all again.”

Kitty was about to say, “Fetch it yourself,” but she remembered her two remarkable leaps.

“I will help you,” she said, not very graciously.

The minute she consented, the shoes became wonderfully light. They carried her after the flying moss in three beautiful bounds—one over the ditch, one across a bed of nettles, and one to the foot of an elm. Kitty gathered every bit, brought it to Robin, and helped him lay a soft green roof upon his house.

“That was splendid!” said Robin. “You jumped like a grasshopper.”

Kitty was pleased. She began to suspect that the shoes were much more agreeable when she was agreeable herself.

At dinner there was chicken pie, followed by a fine plum cake. Kitty ate all that was proper; but afterward, finding herself alone in the dining-room, she saw the cake still standing upon the sideboard.

“I should like just one more slice,” she murmured. “Nobody will know.”

She crept toward it. The shoes crept also, so gently that she believed they meant to oblige her. She stretched out her hand.

At that instant both shoes sprang backward. Kitty flew across the room and sat down suddenly upon the sofa.

She tried again. Once more, just as her fingers approached the sugary top, the shoes skipped away.

“You hateful things!” she exclaimed. “It is my mamma’s cake, and I am sure she would give me some.”

Then you should ask her, the tapping heels seemed to say.

Kitty went to the piazza, where mamma was sewing.

“May I have another piece of cake?”

“No, dear; you have had enough.”

“I thought you would say so,” Kitty muttered.

“Will you carry these peas to the kitchen?”

Kitty frowned. “I suppose I must.”

The shoes walked, but they moved heavily, dragging at every step.

Mamma watched her and smiled a little.

“Try saying, ‘I shall be glad to do it.’”

“I shall be glad to do it,” repeated Kitty, though at first she did not mean it.

Immediately the shoes pranced down the passage. Kitty could scarcely help laughing; and when Cook thanked her, she felt so much happier than she had felt while stealing toward the cake that her good words became almost true.

In the afternoon Nursey asked her to fetch a little frock from the clothes-line, for dark clouds were gathering.

“I want to finish my doll’s bonnet.”

A drop of rain struck the window.

“The frock will be wet,” said Nursey.

“I can’t go this minu—”

Whisk! The shoes carried Kitty into the garden. They raced between the first large drops, leaped over the currant bushes, and stopped under the clothes-line. Kitty snatched down the frock; then the shoes turned and bounded back to the house just as the shower poured upon the gravel.

“Safe and dry!” said Nursey. “Thank you, my pet.”

Kitty looked at the little frock. It belonged to her baby sister, and she was glad it had not been spoiled.

When the rain passed, mamma called Kitty into her room. Upon the bed lay several parcels: some outgrown clothes, two books, a loaf of bread, a jar of broth, and a small purse.

“These are for families who need them,” said mamma. “Mrs. Green is ill, the Miller children have few books, and old Thomas cannot walk to the village. I had intended to send John, but he is busy with papa’s horse. Will you carry the parcels?”

Kitty looked at the heap. Mrs. Green lived beyond the meadow; the Millers lived near the hill; and old Thomas had a cottage at the edge of the wood.

“Must I?” she asked.

“No,” said mamma quietly. “This time you may choose. The parcels can wait until John is free.”

Kitty glanced down at the red shoes. They were perfectly still. Their buttons did not wink; their heels did not tap. She could refuse, and no one would whisk her away.

Then she thought of Mrs. Green lying ill, of the Miller children with nothing new to read, and of old Thomas waiting alone in his cottage. She also remembered Robin’s mossy house, the dry little frock, and the pleasant lightness that came whenever she tried to be useful.

“Yes, mamma,” she said. “I will take them, and I will go now.”

Before mamma could kiss her, the shoes danced three times round the room. They did not drag Kitty or hurry her against her will; they seemed only to share her gladness.

First she went to Mrs. Green’s cottage with the clothes and broth. The pale mother thanked her, while three hungry little children gathered round the loaf like young birds in a nest.

Then Kitty carried the books to the Millers. The children shouted with delight over the pictures, and one of them gave her a bunch of pinks from his tiny garden.

Last of all she visited old Thomas, to whom she gave the purse and a packet of tea.

“Bless your kind heart,” said the old man.

Kitty knew her heart had not always been kind; but she hoped it was growing better. People commonly feel happy after doing happy-making things for others, and Kitty’s face shone all the way down the lane.

When all the errands were done, she found herself near the grove which the village children called Fairyland. It was a green, cosey place, with ferny arches, moss-covered stones, wood flowers, and a brook that talked all day over its pebbles.

“I should like to go in,” said Kitty, “if there is time.”

The shoes gave an approving tap and carried her under the hazel boughs.

No sooner had she entered than she heard a squirrel chattering overhead.

“Here is the red-footed child,” he said. “She helped the small builder whose house had a moss roof.”

Kitty stopped in astonishment.

“Can I understand you?”

“To-day you can,” replied the squirrel, flourishing his tail. “Midsummer makes many strange things plain.”

A robin hopped upon a twig.

“She did not steal the cake,” he sang.

“I tried to,” Kitty confessed.

“But you did not take it,” said the robin; “and resisting the second wrong is better than committing it because one has begun the first.”

A procession of ants crossed the path, each carrying a crumb or a seed.

“We work willingly,” said the foremost ant. “That is why our burdens seem light.”

“You are very small to give lessons,” Kitty observed.

“Good lessons do not need long legs,” answered the ant, and marched away.

Beside the brook sat a green frog, dressed in a shining coat.

“Never kick down another person’s house,” he croaked. “A house is important to the creature who owns it, whether it is built of bricks, sticks, or mud.”

“I did not kick Robin’s down.”

“No; your shoes had more sense than your temper.”

This was rather a saucy speech, but Kitty could not deny it.

Butterflies danced above the foxgloves; bees hummed among the clover bells; a field mouse peeped from beneath a leaf and told her where his babies slept. Kitty walked carefully, lest she tread upon any of the innocent and interesting little creatures whose voices had suddenly become as plain as her own.

At last the woodland musicians began a midsummer dance. The thrush sang, the brook tinkled, the woodpecker beat time, and the grasshoppers played their tiny fiddles.

The red shoes tapped once, twice, three times.

Kitty lifted her arms, and away she went—waltzing over the moss, turning beneath the ferns, and springing over stones as lightly as an india-rubber ball. Never had she danced so gracefully. The squirrels clapped their paws; the birds sang louder; even the solemn frog cried, “Bravo!”

Then the sun dropped toward the hills, red and round, like the sleepy eye of a giant preparing to wink.

At the last golden ray, the music softened. The voices of the creatures became chirps, croaks, rustles, and songs once more. Kitty’s shoes gave a final gentle tap and were only pretty red shoes again.

She walked home in the dusk, carrying her bunch of pinks.

The next morning, when mamma asked her to help Nursey, Kitty nearly said, “I can’t.” But she looked at the silent shoes and remembered.

“I will,” she said instead.

No magic whisked her away; she went by herself, which was better.

Kitty did not become perfect in a day, for children’s habits do not vanish as quickly as fairy enchantments. Yet she grew more obedient, useful, and kind. She learned to dance beautifully, because cheerful feet soon learn graceful ways; and she never again wished to injure another child’s work.

All her life she loved the birds, beasts, insects, and quiet creatures of the woods and fields. She could no longer understand their words, but she had learned to understand their needs.

And though the red shoes never winked again, Kitty sometimes fancied, when she ran pleasantly upon an errand, that their little heels tapped out this tune:

“Willing feet go light and fast;
Kindly deeds bring joy at last.”

## The Cartographer of Lost Roads

On the morning the road disappeared, Mara Venn was painting a river that did not exist.

She sat at the long oak table in the Royal Office of Maps, bent over a sheet of calfskin. Around her, twenty cartographers worked in reverent silence. Their pens scratched like mice behind walls. Dust drifted through shafts of winter sunlight, and the room smelled of ink, sealing wax, and damp wool.

Mara’s river curved through a green valley on the northern frontier. It was a graceful thing, fed by three mountain streams and crossed by a stone bridge at Bellweather. She had drawn it from a surveyor’s notes and colored it with crushed lapis.

Master Vale stopped behind her.

“You’ve made the western bank too wide,” he said.

“The survey gives no measurement.”

“Then use judgment.”

“My judgment says rivers flood.”

“Maps are not made for floods. They are made for certainty.”

He placed one finger on the painted river. When he lifted it, a blue crescent stained his skin.

Across the room, the brass bell above the entrance rang.

A courier stood in the doorway, shivering inside a snow-dusted cloak. “Message from His Majesty’s Third Regiment,” he announced. “For the Master Cartographer.”

Vale broke the seal. His eyes moved swiftly over the page, then returned to the beginning and moved more slowly.

“What is it?” asked someone.

Vale folded the message. “The regiment cannot find the road to Aster.”

A few cartographers smiled, thinking this a joke. The road to Aster was one of the oldest in the kingdom. It ran west from the capital through five villages, crossed the River Ell at Greywake Bridge, and climbed into the high country. Every schoolchild knew it.

“Snow?” suggested a junior mapmaker.

“The road is gone,” said Vale.

The smiles vanished.

According to the courier, the soldiers had followed the king’s highway to the village of Torren. Beyond the last cottage, the milestones ended. The ditches narrowed, the paving stones sank beneath unbroken grass, and within half a mile there was no road at all—only a field of white flowers, blooming in the heart of winter.

The regiment had tried to cross the field. After three hours, they found themselves back at Torren.

Vale went directly to the palace.

By noon, he returned with a royal order.

“We are to correct the maps,” he said.

Mara looked up. “Correct them how?”

“The Aster road is to be removed from every official chart.”

“But it was there yesterday.”

“And today it is not.”

“Then where is Aster?”

Vale’s expression hardened. “A map concerns what can be reached, Apprentice Venn. Not what people wish to reach.”

For three days, the cartographers scraped away the road. On small maps, it took a single stroke of a knife. On the Great Western Survey, the work required painstaking care. Towns that had once stood beside the highway were shifted to lesser lanes. Greywake Bridge was relabeled a ruin. The city of Aster remained in the mountains, but without a road it seemed to float there like an island.

Mara did as she was told.

On the fourth morning, Aster disappeared from the maps.

No knife had touched it. No hand had painted over its walls. The city was simply absent, leaving behind a blank patch of parchment.

That same day, the king issued a proclamation: there had never been a city called Aster.

People laughed at first. Then the bells of Saint Orra rang for the dead of a place that supposedly had never existed, and the laughter stopped.

Mara’s mother had been born in Aster.

She kept a wooden box beneath her bed containing a silver comb, three letters, a faded festival ribbon, and a child’s drawing of a house with blue shutters. Her mother had died seven years before, but she had often spoken of the mountain city: its steep streets, its apple orchards, its copper roofs flashing after rain.

Mara carried the box to work.

She found Master Vale alone in the archive, feeding old surveys into the furnace.

“What are you doing?” she demanded.

“Following orders.”

She pulled a half-burned sheet from the pile. It showed the western mountains and part of the Aster road.

Vale seized her wrist. “Put it back.”

“My mother came from there.”

“Your mother came from the west.”

“She came from Aster.”

“No.” His grip tightened. “Listen to me. Words are doors. Names are roads. If a road has closed, you must not keep walking it in your mind.”

Mara stared at him. There was fear in his face, but not confusion.

“You know what happened.”

“I know enough to burn paper.”

The archive fire snapped between them.

“What happens when we erase a place?” Mara asked.

“We do not erase anything. We acknowledge its absence.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is the only one that will keep you alive.”

He pushed the damaged survey into the flames.

That night, Mara returned to the Office of Maps with the archive key she had copied in wax years ago.

The building groaned in the wind. Moonlight silvered the drafting tables and turned the glass ink bottles into rows of dark teeth. She crossed the main hall, opened the archive, and searched the shelves.

All records of Aster were gone.

She checked the cabinet of military charts, then the land deeds, census rolls, and tax surveys. Nothing remained. Even maps drawn before the city’s founding showed a suspicious emptiness in the mountains.

At last she climbed a ladder to the oldest shelf, where worm-eaten atlases slumbered under gray cloth. Behind them, her fingers found a metal ring set into the wall.

She pulled.

A narrow door opened.

Beyond it, stone steps descended into darkness.

Mara lit a candle and went down.

The hidden room beneath the archive was circular. Maps covered its walls, but they were unlike any she had seen. They showed roads without destinations, coastlines shaped like human profiles, forests marked with the dates of dreams. One chart depicted the capital as a cluster of islands. Another showed a single road spiraling inward until it ended at the words YOU ARE HERE.

In the center stood a black table. A book lay open upon it.

The pages were made of thin, pale leather. Names filled them in different hands and inks.

Mara read the final entries.

ASTER ROAD — Closed on the ninth day of winter.

GREYWAKE BRIDGE — Unfastened.

CITY OF ASTER — Taken beyond the margin.

Below them, written less than an hour ago, was another line.

ROYAL OFFICE OF MAPS — Door opened.

The ink was still wet.

Behind her, the hidden door slammed shut.

Mara spun around.

A man stood at the foot of the stairs. He wore a traveler’s coat stitched with hundreds of tiny pockets. Snow rested on his shoulders, though the night outside was clear. His face was ordinary in the unsettling way of a face immediately forgotten.

“You should not be here,” he said.

“Who are you?”

“I maintain the unused ways.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means I am tired, and you have made more work.”

He approached the table and closed the book.

Mara held the candle between them. “Did you take Aster?”

“No.”

“Do you know who did?”

“Yes.”

“Tell me.”

The man studied her. “What do you remember of the city?”

“Copper roofs. Orchards. A bell tower with carved foxes. Blue shutters on my grandmother’s house.”

“Have you seen these things?”

“My mother told me.”

“So you remember a memory.”

“They were real.”

“Real is not the same as safe.”

He moved past her to a map on the wall. It showed the kingdom as Mara knew it, except its roads extended beyond the parchment in all directions, continuing across the stone.

“Long ago,” he said, “people believed roads were only dirt and stone. Then mapmakers began drawing them. Travelers trusted the drawings. Kings built where the maps commanded. Villages prospered or starved according to lines of ink. Eventually, the maps stopped describing the roads.”

“They began deciding them,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

“That’s impossible.”

The traveler gave her a weary look. “You work in a room where impossible things are copied six times before lunch.”

He touched the line leading west. “Every road has two ends. Every boundary has two sides. When your cartographers made the kingdom certain, they made everything beyond it uncertain. The lost paths had to go somewhere. So did the abandoned gates, the forgotten bridges, the doors bricked inside walls.”

“Beyond the margin.”

“That is one name for it.”

“And Aster?”

“Aster opened a road that should have remained closed.”

Mara thought of the winter flowers and the soldiers returning to where they began.

“What was at the other end?”

The traveler’s eyes shifted toward the book. “A place hungry for names.”

A knock sounded above them.

Then another.

Master Vale’s voice came faintly through the hidden door. “Mara?”

She called out, but the traveler covered her mouth with one cold hand.

“Do not answer.”

Vale knocked again. “I know you’re there.”

The door shuddered.

“Mara, listen carefully. Whatever it tells you, do not let it show you a road.”

The traveler smiled without humor. “Your master is late.”

He opened his coat. The inside was not lined with cloth but with distance.

A narrow path stretched between moonlit trees. Snow fell silently upon black branches. Far away, lights burned on a mountainside.

Mara smelled apples.

“Aster,” she whispered.

The traveler stepped into his own coat and stood upon the path. He extended a hand.

“Come and see what remains.”

The hidden door burst open.

Vale rushed down the stairs carrying a lantern and an iron drafting compass. “Don’t!”

Mara took the traveler’s hand.

Cold swallowed her.

For one breath she was falling. For the next, she stood on a snow-covered road beneath a sky crowded with unfamiliar stars.

The traveler released her.

Behind them, a freestanding doorway framed the hidden chamber. Vale leaped through just before it snapped shut, leaving only empty road.

He landed badly and dropped his lantern. Its flame went out in the snow.

“You fool,” he gasped.

Ahead, the city of Aster climbed the mountain.

Its copper roofs were green with age. Empty windows stared down steep streets. White flowers grew between the paving stones, their petals bright as bone. A bell tower rose above the city, and around its crown crouched carved stone foxes.

Mara’s throat tightened.

“It exists.”

“Of course it exists,” Vale said. “That is the problem.”

They entered through an archway without gates.

No voices greeted them. No footsteps sounded beyond their own. Yet the city did not feel empty. Curtains moved behind windows. Shadows crossed doorways. Once, Mara heard a child laugh in an alley, but when she looked, she saw only a red ball rolling uphill.

“Where are the people?” she asked.

The traveler pointed toward the city square.

Thousands stood there.

Men, women, and children were packed shoulder to shoulder, perfectly still. Frost whitened their hair and eyelashes. None wore coats. None breathed.

In front of them stood a stone well.

A black thread rose from its depths and vanished into the sky.

Mara approached the nearest woman. Her face was calm, almost peaceful. A basket hung from one arm, filled with shriveled apples.

“What happened to them?”

“They listened,” said Vale.

“To what?”

The bell rang.

The sound rolled over the square, deep and soft.

The frozen citizens opened their eyes.

All at once, they spoke.

“Mara Venn.”

Her name thundered from a thousand mouths.

Vale drew the iron compass and stabbed its point into the ground. He swept the other leg in a circle around them. Where the metal scratched the stones, a bright line appeared.

“Stay inside,” he ordered.

The people surged forward.

They stopped at the shining boundary, pressing against air. A little boy reached toward Mara. Frost cracked on his cheeks.

“Mara Venn,” he said in her mother’s voice.

She stumbled back.

The black thread above the well trembled.

The traveler stood outside the circle, untouched by the crowd.

“What is in the well?” Mara shouted.

“A mouth,” he replied.

The citizens repeated the word.

“A mouth. A mouth. A mouth.”

Vale gripped Mara’s shoulders. “Do not tell it anything. Not your name, not the capital, not the smallest village you remember. It takes places by learning how to reach them.”

“You wrote my name in the book,” she said to the traveler. “You brought me here.”

“I maintain the unused ways,” he answered. “I did not say for whom.”

The crowd opened around him.

Mara understood then. “You serve it.”

The traveler looked toward the well. “Everyone serves what they feed.”

The bell rang again.

This time Mara saw the sound: a ripple passing through stone, flesh, snow, and sky. The bright circle around them dimmed. Vale’s compass cracked.

He seized her hand. “We have to make a road back.”

“With what?”

“You’re a cartographer.”

“I need paper.”

“You are standing on a city.”

Mara stared at the square. Its paving stones formed a vast, pale surface broken by dark seams.

Vale thrust the broken compass into her hand. “Draw.”

She knelt and carved a line into the frost.

“Not a road to the Office,” Vale warned. “Not to the capital. If this thing learns the way—”

“I know.”

The citizens pressed closer. The little boy spoke again in her mother’s voice.

“Mara, take me home.”

Her hand faltered.

She knew it was not her mother. Yet the voice held every remembered tenderness: bedtime songs, gentle scoldings, laughter in the kitchen. For one dangerous moment, Mara wanted to answer.

Instead, she carved a bend in the line.

A road needed two ends.

She could not lead it to any named place. She thought of every map she had made, every hill, harbor, and field fixed under her pen. All were known. All could be followed.

Then she remembered the river she had been painting when the Aster road disappeared—the river whose western bank she had made too wide.

A river from a surveyor’s notes. A bridge at Bellweather. A valley rendered in green.

She had never been there.

Perhaps no one had.

Master Vale had told her to use judgment, and she had drawn a floodplain wider than the evidence allowed. In doing so, she had left a small wedge of land between river and mountain without road, village, boundary, or name.

A place uncertain enough to escape into.

She drew the river first. The broken compass scratched twin curves in the frost. She added the bridge, the valley, and the exaggerated western bank. At the edge of the square, space folded. Snow became green grass. Water flashed under sunlight.

The crowd screamed.

The sound was not human. Windows shattered throughout Aster.

“Go!” Vale shouted.

Mara ran toward the opening, but he did not follow.

She turned.

The black thread had bent toward the map. It quivered above the newly drawn road like a needle finding north.

Vale planted himself between the well and the opening.

“Come on!”

“If the road remains, it will follow.”

“Then we close it from the other side.”

“It has a thousand voices and now it knows yours.”

The traveler watched from the steps of the bell tower.

Vale pulled a small bottle of red ink from his coat.

Mara knew that bottle. Every master cartographer carried one. Red ink was used only for final borders: lines the Crown declared permanent.

Vale poured it across the road behind her.

A crimson wall rose from the stones.

The people of Aster threw themselves against it. Vale stood on the far side, surrounded by their pale hands and open mouths.

“Mara!” he called.

She pressed both palms to the barrier.

He looked older than he had that morning. Older and less afraid.

“Maps are not made for certainty,” he said. “I was wrong.”

The black thread curled around his wrist.

“What are they made for?” she cried.

Vale smiled.

“Return.”

He dragged the red line across the road.

The opening closed.

Mara fell onto wet grass.

For several minutes she lay beside the blue river, listening to its current. The sky was warm and cloudless. Tiny yellow flowers nodded along the bank.

There was no snow, no city, no crowd.

In her fist she held the broken compass.

Mara followed the river downstream. By evening she reached the stone bridge at Bellweather.

There was no village nearby, only an abandoned surveyor’s camp. Inside one of the tents she found moldy blankets, rusted instruments, and a leather case containing field notes.

Most were unreadable. The final page said:

No river found. Valley dry. Returning east tomorrow.

Mara walked for six days before she reached a road she recognized.

During her absence, the kingdom had changed.

No one remembered Master Vale. At the Royal Office of Maps, his room belonged to a woman named Mistress Arlen, who claimed to have held the position for eleven years. The hidden door in the archive opened onto a brick wall.

Aster remained absent.

Mara’s box still lay beneath her bed, but the letters inside were blank, the silver comb had become bone, and the child’s drawing showed a house without windows.

Only the festival ribbon was unchanged. Woven into its faded fabric were copper foxes and the words ASTER IN BLOOM.

Mara returned to work.

She was no longer an apprentice; according to the Office records, she had been promoted months earlier. No one thought this strange.

At her old table, the unfinished northern map waited. The blue river gleamed across the valley, exactly as she had painted it. Yet now Bellweather Bridge bore a small black mark beside it.

A figure stood there, drawn in ink.

He wore a traveler’s coat.

Mara leaned closer.

The figure raised its head.

She snatched up a knife and cut him from the map. The scrap writhed in her hand. She carried it to the furnace and watched until it curled into ash.

Then she returned to the table.

For many years, Mara served the Crown as a cartographer. She mapped islands, forests, deserts, and war-torn borders. She became famous for leaving certain spaces unfinished.

“Errors,” complained royal ministers.

“Possibilities,” she replied.

She drew roads with gentle curves, so travelers could see what they approached. She marked old paths even when weeds covered them. On every map she included a small blank place without a name.

Those blank places saved lives.

People lost in blizzards sometimes stumbled into warm valleys absent from every local chart. Sailors wrecked in storms washed onto islands that had not been there the day before. Children fleeing wolves found bridges over rivers where no bridge had stood.

They returned with strange stories and white flowers in their pockets.

Years passed. The king died, and his daughter took the throne. The Royal Office filled with younger cartographers who had never heard of Aster. They used new instruments and laughed at superstition. Their lines were beautifully straight.

One winter morning, an apprentice brought Mara a map of the western mountains.

“We found an error, Master Venn,” he said.

Mara was old then. Her hands trembled, and she could no longer paint a line without resting her wrist.

“What error?”

The apprentice pointed to a blank patch of parchment.

“There should be something here.”

“Should there?”

“The surrounding roads turn away from it. That implies deliberate omission.”

“Then perhaps omission was wise.”

He smiled politely. Young people often smiled that way when they believed age had made her foolish.

“We sent surveyors.”

Mara looked up sharply.

“They returned this morning,” he continued. “There’s a city in the mountains. Abandoned, apparently. Copper roofs, apple orchards, a bell tower decorated with foxes.”

The room seemed to tilt.

“Did they enter?”

“No. They found this on the road.”

He placed a wooden box on her table.

Inside lay an iron drafting compass, broken at the hinge.

Beneath it was a folded scrap of paper.

Mara opened the note.

The handwriting belonged to Master Vale.

A road has two ends.

Below the words, he had drawn a door.

The apprentice leaned over her shoulder. “Where does it lead?”

From somewhere very far away, a bell began to ring.

Mara took up her pen.

“To someone who has been waiting,” she said.

She dipped the nib in red ink and drew a line through the door.

Outside, snow began to fall. Across the kingdom, roads vanished beneath it—royal highways, hunters’ tracks, alleys, garden paths—until every route looked blank and every traveler had to choose the way anew.

And in the western mountains, where no official map admitted a city, copper roofs shone beneath the moon.

A gate opened.

An old man stepped through, carrying a lantern.

Behind him came the lost people of Aster, blinking as if waking from a long sleep. They descended through the orchards and followed a road that appeared beneath their feet one stone at a time.

At its distant end, Mara waited with a fresh sheet of paper.

This time, she left the margin open.
